hints: Focus on the word two in the options. Resolution is always about telling two very close points apart, not about one object alone.
Think minimum apart, not maximum apart. Ask yourself, how close can two dots get before they blur into one?
walkthrough:
**Picture what resolution really means**

Imagine two tiny dots very close together under the microscope. At first you see two separate dots.

Now move them closer and closer. At some point they blur into one fuzzy blob. That tipping point is resolution.

**Lock in the precise Cambridge definition**

Resolution is not just general sharpness. It is a measurable distance.

It is the smallest separation between two objects that still lets you see them as two separate objects.

**Match to the option**

Only option C says minimum distance that allows two objects to be viewed as separate. That is the exact definition, so C is the answer.

options.A: This sounds nice but it is too vague. Sharpness describes image quality, not the measured minimum distance between two points.
options.B: This describes the diameter of the field of view, the widest area you can see at once, not resolution.
options.C: This is exactly right. Resolution is the minimum distance apart two objects must be to still be distinguished as separate.
options.D: Seeing a single tiny object is detection, not resolution. Resolution always needs two objects and the gap between them.
